claims.source: The PopZ polar organizing protein is thought to assemble a porous homo-polymeric matrix at the cell poles that captures the segregated ParB•parS complex (Figure 1A) via a direct interaction with ParAB (Bowman et al., 2008, 2013; Ebersbach et al., 2008; Holmes et al., 2016; Laloux and Jacobs-Wagner, 2013).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: PopZ captures the segregated ParB•parS complex via a direct interaction with ParAB.
claims.source: The PopZ polar organizing protein is thought to assemble a porous homo-polymeric matrix at the cell poles that captures the segregated ParB•parS complex (Figure 1A) via a direct interaction with ParAB (Bowman et al., 2008, 2013; Ebersbach et al., 2008; Holmes et al., 2016; Laloux and Jacobs-Wagner, 2013).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: In newborn cells PopZ is localized to the old cell pole, whereas the newborn pole initially lacks a PopZ cluster.
claims.source: The polar localization of PopZ is cell cycle-regulated: in newborn cells PopZ is localized to the old cell pole, whereas the newborn pole initially lacks a PopZ cluster (Bowman et al., 2008; Ebersbach et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: During S-phase, PopZ adopts a bipolar disposition coincident with ParB•parS segregation.
claims.source: During S-phase, PopZ adopts a bipolar disposition (Figure 1A) coincident with ParB•parS segregation to facilitate its capture at the opposite pole.
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claims.claim: Formation of the second polar PopZ cluster may depend on the ParA ATPase and the TipN landmark protein.
claims.source: Formation of the second polar PopZ cluster may depend on the ParA ATPase and the TipN landmark protein, a coiled-coil protein that interacts with ParA and that marks the new pole as flagellar assembly site (Huitema et al., 2006; Laloux and Jacobs-Wagner, 2013; Lam et al., 2006; Ptacin et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis supported by citations.

claims.claim: TipN is a coiled-coil protein that interacts with ParA and marks the new pole as flagellar assembly site.
claims.source: Formation of the second polar PopZ cluster may depend on the ParA ATPase and the TipN landmark protein, a coiled-coil protein that interacts with ParA and that marks the new pole as flagellar assembly site (Huitema et al., 2006; Laloux and Jacobs-Wagner, 2013; Lam et al., 2006; Ptacin et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: ParAB are essential for viability in C. crescentus.
claims.source: Although ParAB are essential for viability in C. crescentus, TipN or PopZ are individually dispensable (Bowman et al., 2008; Ebersbach et al., 2008; Huitema et al., 2006; Lam et al., 2006; Mohl and Gober, 1997), but joint inactivation of both genes arrests growth (Schofield et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: TipN or PopZ are individually dispensable in C. crescentus.
claims.source: Although ParAB are essential for viability in C. crescentus, TipN or PopZ are individually dispensable (Bowman et al., 2008; Ebersbach et al., 2008; Huitema et al., 2006; Lam et al., 2006; Mohl and Gober, 1997), but joint inactivation of both genes arrests growth (Schofield et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Joint inactivation of TipN and PopZ arrests growth in C. crescentus.
claims.source: Although ParAB are essential for viability in C. crescentus, TipN or PopZ are individually dispensable (Bowman et al., 2008; Ebersbach et al., 2008; Huitema et al., 2006; Lam et al., 2006; Mohl and Gober, 1997), but joint inactivation of both genes arrests growth (Schofield et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citation.

claims.claim: Most α-proteobacterial genomes encode PopZ and ParAB, but not TipN.
claims.source: As most α-proteobacterial genomes encode PopZ and ParAB, but not TipN, TipN-independent control mechanism(s) for PopZ polarization should exist in α-proteobacteria.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observation that leads to an inference.

claims.claim: TipN-independent control mechanism(s) for PopZ polarization should exist in α-proteobacteria.
claims.source: As most α-proteobacterial genomes encode PopZ and ParAB, but not TipN, TipN-independent control mechanism(s) for PopZ polarization should exist in α-proteobacteria.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an inference based on genomic observations.

claims.claim: In the Rhizobiales order, PopZ does not appear to fasten ParB at the cell poles as polar PopZ does not co-localize with ParB.
claims.source: In the Rhizobiales order of the α-proteobacteria, PopZ does not appear to fasten ParB at the cell poles as polar PopZ does not co-localize with ParB: while PopZ is monopolar, ParB localizes in a bipolar fashion (Deghelt et al., 2014; Grangeon et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: In Rhizobiales, PopZ is monopolar while ParB localizes in a bipolar fashion.
claims.source: In the Rhizobiales order of the α-proteobacteria, PopZ does not appear to fasten ParB at the cell poles as polar PopZ does not co-localize with ParB: while PopZ is monopolar, ParB localizes in a bipolar fashion (Deghelt et al., 2014; Grangeon et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: PopZ has undergone functional specialization in the Rhizobiales, presumably interacting with other (unknown) client proteins.
claims.source: Thus, compared to the bipolar co-localization of PopZ and ParB observed in C. crescentus (Bowman et al., 2008; Ebersbach et al., 2008; Ptacin et al., 2014), PopZ seems to have undergone functional specialization in the Rhizobiales, presumably interacting with other (unknown) client proteins.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an inference based on localization differences.

claims.claim: The genomes of the obligate intracellular (rickettsial) lineage encode PopZ and ParAB orthologs.
claims.source: The genomes of the obligate intracellular (rickettsial) lineage also encode PopZ and ParAB orthologs (Andersson et al., 1998), but not several other known client proteins of C. crescentus PopZ that depend on a short N-terminal stretch in PopZ to interact with it (Bowman et al., 2010; Holmes et al., 2016; Laloux and Jacobs-Wagner, 2013; Ptacin et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Rickettsial genomes do not encode several other known client proteins of C. crescentus PopZ that depend on a short N-terminal stretch in PopZ to interact with it.
claims.source: The genomes of the obligate intracellular (rickettsial) lineage also encode PopZ and ParAB orthologs (Andersson et al., 1998), but not several other known client proteins of C. crescentus PopZ that depend on a short N-terminal stretch in PopZ to interact with it (Bowman et al., 2010; Holmes et al., 2016; Laloux and Jacobs-Wagner, 2013; Ptacin et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: There is a reciprocal, physical and conserved interaction between PopZ and the cytoplasmic N-terminal zinc-finger domain (ZnR) from ZitP.
claims.source: Here, we unearth a reciprocal, physical and conserved interaction between PopZ and the cytoplasmic N-terminal zinc-finger domain (ZnR) from ZitP (Hughes et al., 2010), a bifunctional and bipolar membrane protein whose C-terminal DUF3426 domain is required for polar pilus biogenesis (Mignolet et al., 2016)(Christen et al., 2016), but dispensable for motility.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding of the study.

claims.claim: ZitP is a bifunctional and bipolar membrane protein.
claims.source: Here, we unearth a reciprocal, physical and conserved interaction between PopZ and the cytoplasmic N-terminal zinc-finger domain (ZnR) from ZitP (Hughes et al., 2010), a bifunctional and bipolar membrane protein whose C-terminal DUF3426 domain is required for polar pilus biogenesis (Mignolet et al., 2016)(Christen et al., 2016), but dispensable for motility.
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: The C-terminal DUF3426 domain of ZitP is required for polar pilus biogenesis.
claims.source: Here, we unearth a reciprocal, physical and conserved interaction between PopZ and the cytoplasmic N-terminal zinc-finger domain (ZnR) from ZitP (Hughes et al., 2010), a bifunctional and bipolar membrane protein whose C-terminal DUF3426 domain is required for polar pilus biogenesis (Mignolet et al., 2016)(Christen et al., 2016), but dispensable for motility.
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: The C-terminal DUF3426 domain of ZitP is dispensable for motility.
claims.source: Here, we unearth a reciprocal, physical and conserved interaction between PopZ and the cytoplasmic N-terminal zinc-finger domain (ZnR) from ZitP (Hughes et al., 2010), a bifunctional and bipolar membrane protein whose C-terminal DUF3426 domain is required for polar pilus biogenesis (Mignolet et al., 2016)(Christen et al., 2016), but dispensable for motility.
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: The PopZ•ZitP interaction is required to control cytokinesis and centromere positioning from the membrane.
claims.source: We locate the structural determinants governing PopZ•ZitP complex formation and we show that this interaction is required to control cytokinesis and centromere positioning from the membrane.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding of the study.

claims.claim: The PopZ•ZitP interaction does not require the PopZ N-terminal segment that is used by other client proteins.
claims.source: The PopZ•ZitP interaction differs for previously described interactions between PopZ and client proteins (Holmes et al., 2016) in that it does not require the aforementioned PopZ N-terminal segment.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding of the study.

claims.claim: ZitP induces PopZ bipolarity in the heterologous host Escherichia coli.
claims.source: We show that ZitP induces PopZ bipolarity in the heterologous host Escherichia coli and we reconstitute a bipolar ZitP•PopZ•ParB tripartite complex in this system.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding of the study.

claims.claim: A bipolar ZitP•PopZ•ParB tripartite complex can be reconstituted in E. coli.
claims.source: We show that ZitP induces PopZ bipolarity in the heterologous host Escherichia coli and we reconstitute a bipolar ZitP•PopZ•ParB tripartite complex in this system.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding of the study.

claims.claim: The PopZ•ZitP complex is modular.
claims.source: Examining rickettsial PopZ and ZitP orthologs, we find that the PopZ•ZitP complex is modular and that the structure-function relationship is maintained in the obligate intracellular lineage.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding of the study.

claims.claim: The structure-function relationship of the PopZ•ZitP complex is maintained in the obligate intracellular lineage.
claims.source: Examining rickettsial PopZ and ZitP orthologs, we find that the PopZ•ZitP complex is modular and that the structure-function relationship is maintained in the obligate intracellular lineage.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding of the study.

claims.claim: A C. crescentus strain bearing a Tn5-GFP insertion in the 5'-proximal third of the CC_2215/CCNA_02298 gene (zitP) expresses a bipolarly localized and truncated ZitP-GFP fusion protein and is viable.
claims.source: We previously isolated a C. crescentus strain bearing a Tn5-GFP insertion in the 5'-proximal third of the poorly characterized and conserved CC_2215/CCNA_02298 gene (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, dubbed zitP, zinc-finger targeting PopZ, Figure 1B–D). The resulting strain expresses a bipolarly localized and truncated ZitP-GFP fusion protein and is viable (Hughes et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a previous finding supported by citation.

claims.claim: Genome-wide transposon insertion sequencing (Tn-Seq) revealed that ZitP is not essential for viability, but required for pilus biogenesis and motility.
claims.source: Consistent with this result, genome-wide transposon insertion sequencing (Tn-Seq) revealed that ZitP is not essential for viability, but required for pilus biogenesis and motility (Christen et al., 2011, 2016; Hughes et al., 2010)(Mignolet et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: The predicted ZitP protein harbors an N-terminal zinc-finger domain (zinc_ribbon_5 or PF13719 superfamily, residues 1–37).
claims.source: The predicted ZitP protein harbors an N-terminal zinc-finger domain (zinc_ribbon_5 or PF13719 superfamily, residues 1–37, henceforth ZnR, Figure 1B–C) and a trans-membrane segment (TM, residues 106–127) preceding the C-terminal DUF3426 (residues 128–245).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a structural prediction.

claims.claim: ZitP has a trans-membrane segment (TM, residues 106–127).
claims.source: The predicted ZitP protein harbors an N-terminal zinc-finger domain (zinc_ribbon_5 or PF13719 superfamily, residues 1–37, henceforth ZnR, Figure 1B–C) and a trans-membrane segment (TM, residues 106–127) preceding the C-terminal DUF3426 (residues 128–245).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a structural prediction.

claims.claim: ZitP has a C-terminal DUF3426 domain (residues 128–245).
claims.source: The predicted ZitP protein harbors an N-terminal zinc-finger domain (zinc_ribbon_5 or PF13719 superfamily, residues 1–37, henceforth ZnR, Figure 1B–C) and a trans-membrane segment (TM, residues 106–127) preceding the C-terminal DUF3426 (residues 128–245).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a structural prediction.

claims.claim: The DUF3426 is required for polar pilus biogenesis but not required for motility or to direct ZitP to the cell poles.
claims.source: While the DUF3426 is required for polar pilus biogenesis (Mignolet et al., 2016), it is not required for motility or to direct ZitP to the cell poles since in polar ZitPTn-GFP the GFP moiety is fused in-frame to codon 49 of ZitP (green triangle in Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding combining previous knowledge and current observation.

claims.claim: Quantitative live-cell fluorescence imaging of ZitPTn-GFP in zitP::Tn5-GFP cells (n = 1048) revealed monopolar fluorescent foci in non-constricted cells, while bipolar foci are present in constricted cells.
claims.source: Quantitative live-cell fluorescence imaging of ZitPTn-GFP in zitP::Tn5-GFP cells (n = 1048) revealed monopolar fluorescent foci in non-constricted cells, while bipolar foci are present in constricted cells (Figure 1D), suggesting that the ZnR and/or adjacent residues are necessary and sufficient for ZitP polarization and that bipolarization is cell cycle-regulated.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding from quantitative imaging data shown in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: The ZnR and/or adjacent residues are necessary and sufficient for ZitP polarization and bipolarization is cell cycle-regulated.
claims.source: Quantitative live-cell fluorescence imaging of ZitPTn-GFP in zitP::Tn5-GFP cells (n = 1048) revealed monopolar fluorescent foci in non-constricted cells, while bipolar foci are present in constricted cells (Figure 1D), suggesting that the ZnR and/or adjacent residues are necessary and sufficient for ZitP polarization and that bipolarization is cell cycle-regulated.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an inference from the imaging data.

claims.claim: Residues 1–90 of ZitP carry the necessary information for polar localization of ZitP.
claims.source: We engineered strains expressing a Dendra2-ZitP(1-90) fusion protein (an N-terminal translational fusion of the Dendra2 fluorescent protein to only the cytoplasmic part of ZitP) from the xylose-inducible promoter (Pxyl) at the xylX locus in the wild-type (WT, NA1000) or ΔzitP background and found an identical localization pattern as for the ZitPTn-GFP strain, indicating that residues 1–90 carry the necessary information for polar localization of ZitP (Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding from localization experiments shown in Figure 1E.

claims.claim: Orthologous Dendra2-ZitP(1-90) variants from other α-proteobacteria show an identical localization pattern when expressed in C. crescentus.
claims.source: To test if polarization is also a feature of ZitP from other α-proteobacteria, we expressed orthologous Dendra2-ZitP(1-90) variants in WT or ΔzitP C. crescentus cells and observed an identical localization pattern of these fusion proteins (Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding from localization experiments shown in Figure 1E.

claims.claim: The zinc-finger domain from the unrelated AgmX protein encoded in the δ-proteobacterium Myxococcus xanthus is not polar in C. crescentus.
claims.source: By contrast, the zinc-finger domain from the unrelated AgmX protein encoded in the δ-proteobacterium Myxococcus xanthus (Nan et al., 2010) is not polar in C. crescentus (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), indicating that the zinc-finger domain of AgmX diverged.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding from localization experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: The 43 residues encompassing the C. crescentus ZitP ZnR domain suffice to direct Dendra2 to the cell poles.
claims.source: Next, we asked if the highly conserved 43 residues encompassing the C. crescentus ZitP ZnR domain (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) suffice to direct Dendra2 to the cell poles. Expression of Dendra2-ZitP(1-43) from xylX in C. crescentus WT or ΔzitP cells indeed gave rise to cell cycle-dependent bipolar fluorescence (Figure 1G)
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding from localization experiments shown in Figure 1G.

claims.claim: Dendra2-ZitP(1-43) is initially monopolar in G1-phase cells and switches to a bipolar disposition during S-phase, 60 min after the release of G1 cells into fresh medium.
claims.source: This ZnR interacts directly with PopZ and controls its localization from the membrane, even when PopZ no longer carries the interaction sites for ParAB, indicating that PopZ localization is regulated by redundant mechanisms in C. crescentus.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding from time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 1G.

claims.claim: mCherry-PopZ co-localizes with Dendra2-ZitP(1-43) in ΔzitP cells.
claims.source: Since this cell cycle localization pattern of Dendra2-ZitP(1-43) closely resembles that of the polar matrix protein PopZ (Bowman et al., 2008; Ebersbach et al., 2008), we co-expressed Dendra2-ZitP(1-43) and mCherry-PopZ in ΔzitP (xylX::dendra-zitP1-43popZ::mCherry-popZ) cells and found that mCherry-PopZ co-localizes with Dendra2-ZitP(1-43) (Figure 1H).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding from co-localization experiments shown in Figure 1H.

claims.claim: ZitPTn-GFP, Dendra2-ZitP(1-90) and Dendra2-ZitP(1-43) are all delocalized (diffuse) in ΔpopZ cells.
claims.source: Importantly, ZitPTn-GFP, Dendra2-ZitP(1-90) and Dendra2-ZitP(1-43) are all delocalized (diffuse) in ΔpopZ cells (Figure 1D, E and F) and immunoblotting revealed that the abundance of Dendra2-ZitP(1-43) is not significantly affected by the ΔpopZ mutation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding from localization experiments shown in Figures 1D, E, F and immunoblotting in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: The abundance of Dendra2-ZitP(1-43) is not significantly affected by the ΔpopZ mutation.
claims.source: Importantly, ZitPTn-GFP, Dendra2-ZitP(1-90) and Dendra2-ZitP(1-43) are all delocalized (diffuse) in ΔpopZ cells (Figure 1D, E and F) and immunoblotting revealed that the abundance of Dendra2-ZitP(1-43) is not significantly affected by the ΔpopZ mutation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding from immunoblotting shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: Dendra2-ZitP(1-43) and full length Dendra2-ZitP adopt a monopolar 'plug'-like disposition when PopZ is overexpressed.
claims.source: We observed Dendra2-ZitP(1-43) and full length Dendra2-ZitP to adopt a monopolar 'plug'-like disposition when PopZ is overexpressed (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that Dendra2-ZitP(1-43) is indeed recruited to PopZ 'plugs'.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding from localization experiments shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: ZitP(1-43) and PopZ can be co-purified by SEC and the resulting ZitP(1-43)•PopZ complex has a high apparent molecular mass.
claims.source: ZitP(1-43) and PopZ can be co-purified by SEC and the resulting ZitP(1-43)•PopZ complex has a high apparent molecular mass, suggesting that ZitP binds oligomeric PopZ.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding from SEC experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B-D.

claims.claim: ZitP binds oligomeric PopZ.
claims.source: ZitP(1-43) and PopZ can be co-purified by SEC and the resulting ZitP(1-43)•PopZ complex has a high apparent molecular mass, suggesting that ZitP binds oligomeric PopZ.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an inference from SEC data.

claims.claim: Isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC) estimated the dissociation constant (KD) between ZitP(1-43) and PopZ at 700 nM.
claims.source: Isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC) estimated the dissociation constant (KD) between ZitP(1-43) and PopZ at 700 nM (Figure 2C), confirming the specific interaction between both proteins in vitro.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding from ITC experiments shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: The 20 NMR structures of ZitP(1-43) were overlaid with a root mean square deviation of 0.23 Å over the backbone atoms.
claims.source: The 20 NMR structures of ZitP(1-43) were overlaid with a root mean square deviation of 0.23 Å over the backbone atoms (Supplementary file 1), revealing two double-stranded antiparallel β-sheets (ββαββ), forming a 'crab claw' in which C5, C8, C28, C31 are located at the turns of β1/β2 and β3/β4 chelate a zinc ion (Figure 2D–E).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding from NMR structure determination shown in Figure 2D-E and Supplementary file 1.

claims.claim: The ZitP ZnR structure reveals two double-stranded antiparallel β-sheets (ββαββ), forming a 'crab claw' in which C5, C8, C28, C31 chelate a zinc ion.
claims.source: The 20 NMR structures of ZitP(1-43) were overlaid with a root mean square deviation of 0.23 Å over the backbone atoms (Supplementary file 1), revealing two double-stranded antiparallel β-sheets (ββαββ), forming a 'crab claw' in which C5, C8, C28, C31 are located at the turns of β1/β2 and β3/β4 chelate a zinc ion (Figure 2D–E).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding from NMR structure determination shown in Figure 2D-E.

claims.claim: The ZitP ZnR structure is unusual, though related to the family of the 'ribbon zinc-fingers' (zinc_ribbon_5 or PF13719 superfamily), albeit it lacks the additional β-strand typically located in between the two β-sheets.
claims.source: This ZitP ZnR structure is unusual, though related to the family of the 'ribbon zinc-fingers' (zinc_ribbon_5 or PF13719 superfamily), albeit it lacks the additional β-strand typically located in between the two β-sheets.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the structural data.

claims.claim: W35 in ZitP is required to bind PopZ in vitro, as determined by ITC with a W35I mutant derivative of ZitP(1-43).
claims.source: Moreover, W35 is surrounded by a surface-exposed patch of basic residues (K18, R24, R27, R34, Figure 2E) and it is required to bind PopZ in vitro, as determined by ITC with a W35I mutant derivative of ZitP(1-43) [ZitP(1-43)W35I, Figure 2C].
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding from ITC experiments shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: W35I impairs the interaction of Dendra2-ZitP(1-43) with polar PopZ in vivo.
claims.source: Consistent with these ITC experiments, W35I impairs the interaction of Dendra2-ZitP(1-43) with polar PopZ in vivo (Figure 3A and B), as indicated by the diffuse fluorescence of Dendra2-ZitP(1-43) in C. crescentus and in E. coli cells expressing PopZ (Figure 3A–B).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding from localization experiments shown in Figure 3A-B.

claims.claim: A C5S/C8S/C28S/C31S quadruple or a R24A/R27A double mutation both disrupt polarization of Dendra2-ZitP(1-43) in C. crescentus and in PopZ-expressing E. coli cells.
claims.source: Similarly, a C5S/C8S/C28S/C31S quadruple or a R24A/R27A double mutation both disrupt polarization of Dendra2-ZitP(1-43) in C. crescentus and in PopZ-expressing E. coli cells (Figure 3A–B).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding from localization experiments shown in Figure 3A-B.

claims.claim: All of the substituted Dendra2-ZitP(1-43) variants are stably expressed.
claims.source: As all of the substituted Dendra2-ZitP(1-43) variants are stably expressed (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), we conclude that these residues are required for the formation of a polar ZitP(1-43)•PopZ complex.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding from immunoblotting shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: W35, the basic patch and the integrity of the Zn2+ coordinating center are required for the formation of a polar ZitP(1-43)•PopZ complex.
claims.source: As all of the substituted Dendra2-ZitP(1-43) variants are stably expressed (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), we conclude that these residues are required for the formation of a polar ZitP(1-43)•PopZ complex.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the mutagenesis and localization data.

claims.claim: R. sphaeroides Dendra2-ZitP(1-43) is largely diffuse in C. crescentus or in PopZ-expressing E. coli, but some faint polar signals are noticeable.
claims.source: Interestingly, R. sphaeroides Dendra2-ZitP(1-43) is also largely diffuse in C. crescentus (Figure 3C) or in PopZ-expressing E. coli, but some faint polar signals are noticeable as well (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding from localization experiments shown in Figure 3C-D.

claims.claim: The 'corrected' R. sphaeroides ZitP(1-43)Q27R version is robustly polar in C. crescentus and in PopZ-expressing E. coli cells.
claims.source: We therefore asked if polar localization could be improved if this substitution is 'corrected' (i.e. reversed) by a Q27R substitution of R. sphaeroides Dendra2-ZitP(1-43). This 'corrected' R. sphaeroides ZitP(1-43)Q27R version is indeed robustly polar in C. crescentus (Figure 3C) and in PopZ-expressing E. coli cells (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding from localization experiments shown in Figure 3C-D.

claims.claim: When the W35I substitution is introduced into the 'corrected' R. sphaeroides variant, polar localization is again lost without compromising abundance.
claims.source: When the W35I substitution is introduced into this 'corrected' R. sphaeroides variant, polar localization is again lost without compromising abundance (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding from localization and immunoblotting experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: ChIP-Seq experiments confirmed that ParB exclusively occupies the parS site in vivo.
claims.source: To this end, we conducted chromatin immunoprecipitation-deep-sequencing (ChIP-Seq) using antibodies recognizing ParB (anti-ParB) or ZitP (anti-ZitP specific for either the N-terminus or the C-terminus, Figure 4—figure supplement 1). These experiments confirmed that ParB exclusively occupies the parS site in vivo
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding from ChIP-Seq experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The ZitP•PopZ complex associates with two chromosomal regions flanking, but not overlapping, parS (by 2–3 kpb).
claims.source: These experiments confirmed that ParB exclusively occupies the parS site in vivo and additionally showed that i) the ZitP•PopZ complex associates with two chromosomal regions flanking, but not overlapping, parS (by 2–3 kpb) and that ii) the ParAB interaction sites in PopZ are critical for this association (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding from ChIP-Seq experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The ParAB interaction sites in PopZ are critical for the association of the ZitP•PopZ complex with chromosomal regions flanking parS.
claims.source: These experiments confirmed that ParB exclusively occupies the parS site in vivo and additionally showed that i) the ZitP•PopZ complex associates with two chromosomal regions flanking, but not overlapping, parS (by 2–3 kpb) and that ii) the ParAB interaction sites in PopZ are critical for this association (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding from ChIP-Seq experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Inactivation of ZitP has a mild effect on CFP-ParB localization in WT cells.
claims.source: While inactivation of ZitP has a mild effect on CFP-ParB localization in WT cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), we observed aberrant CFP-ParB localization and perturbed cytokinesis in ΔzitP cells expressing variants of PopZ impaired in binding ParB and/or ParA (Laloux and Jacobs-Wagner, 2013; Ptacin et al., 2014)(Figure 4A).

results.result: The NMR solution structure of the ZitP zinc-finger domain (ZnR, residues 1-43) was determined, revealing an unusual ββαββ 'crab claw' architecture with four cysteine residues (C5, C8, C28, C31) coordinating a zinc ion. The structure has a root mean square deviation of 0.23 Å over backbone atoms and is related to the zinc_ribbon_5 superfamily but lacks a typical β-strand.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C66, C67, and C68 collectively describe the NMR structure determination with appropriate structural detail and precision metrics (RMSD). The structure is supported by data shown in Figure 2D-E and Supplementary file 1, with proper characterization of secondary structure elements and zinc coordination.

results.result: ZitP(1-43) directly interacts with PopZ with a dissociation constant (KD) of 700 nM as measured by isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC). The proteins co-purify by size exclusion chromatography as a high molecular mass complex, suggesting ZitP binds oligomeric PopZ. The W35 residue in ZitP is required for PopZ binding in vitro.
results.evaluation: Claims C36, C63, C64, C65, and C69 are well-supported by biochemical data including ITC (Figure 2C), SEC (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B-D), and mutagenesis experiments. The KD value is quantitatively determined, and the requirement for W35 is demonstrated by loss of binding in the W35I mutant.

results.result: The ZitP ZnR domain (residues 1-43) is necessary and sufficient for polar localization in C. crescentus. Quantitative imaging of ZitPTn-GFP (n=1048) showed monopolar foci in non-constricted cells and bipolar foci in constricted cells, indicating cell cycle-regulated bipolarization. Polar localization is completely dependent on PopZ, as all ZitP variants are delocalized in ΔpopZ cells without affecting protein abundance.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C54, C57, C60-C61 are supported by extensive microscopy data (Figures 1D-G) with appropriate sample sizes (n=1048) and controls including ΔpopZ strains and immunoblotting to confirm protein stability. The cell cycle-dependent localization pattern is clearly documented.

results.result: Specific residues in the ZitP ZnR are required for PopZ interaction: W35, the basic patch (R24, R27), and the zinc-coordinating cysteines (C5, C8, C28, C31). Mutations W35I, R24A/R27A, or C5S/C8S/C28S/C31S all disrupt polar localization in both C. crescentus and E. coli expressing PopZ, while all mutant proteins remain stably expressed.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C73 are supported by systematic mutagenesis with localization assays in two systems (Figures 3A-B) and immunoblotting controls (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A). The convergent evidence from multiple mutations affecting the same phenotype strengthens the conclusion about structural determinants.

results.result: ZitP induces PopZ bipolarity in the heterologous host E. coli, and a bipolar ZitP•PopZ•ParB tripartite complex can be reconstituted in this system. Membrane-anchored ZitP (residues 1-133) robustly controls PopZ localization, directing it to bipolar positions at the cell poles.
results.evaluation: Claims C42, C43, C101, and C106 are supported by heterologous expression experiments in E. coli (Figures 5A-E, 6E) including PALM imaging (Figure 5C) and biochemical fractionation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C). The reconstitution of the tripartite complex (Figure 5D) demonstrates functional conservation.

results.result: ZitP regulates cytokinesis and the localization of ParB and PopZ in C. crescentus. In ΔzitP cells expressing PopZ variants impaired in ParAB binding (PopZKE, PopZΔ26, PopZKEP), aberrant ParB localization, perturbed cytokinesis, and reduced viability are observed. ZitP is important for growth when the ParAB-dependent PopZ localization pathway is impaired, indicating at least two redundant mechanisms control PopZ localization.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C5, C40, C81-C85, C89-C91 are supported by genetic experiments including localization microscopy (Figure 4A), efficiency of plating assays (Figure 4B), and growth measurements (Figure 4C). The synthetic phenotypes in double mutants provide strong evidence for redundant pathways, though the molecular details of the ParAB-dependent pathway remain incompletely defined.

results.result: ZitP targets PopZ independently of the previously known N-terminal binding sites for ParAB and other client proteins. The PopZ•ZitP interaction differs from previously described PopZ-client interactions in that it does not require the PopZ N-terminal segment, underscoring the multivalent interactions of PopZ.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C41, C112, and C115 are supported by experiments with PopZΔ26 and PopZKEP variants that lack or have mutated N-terminal regions (Figures 4A-C, 5—figure supplement 1B). The ability of ZitP to interact with and control these PopZ variants demonstrates independence from the N-terminal region.

results.result: Overexpression of membrane-anchored ZitP(1-133) causes dominant-negative phenotypes including stalled ParB segregation, internal PopZ clusters, displacement of ParA from poles, and cell filamentation. These defects require both membrane anchoring and the ability to bind PopZ (W35), as they are not observed with ZitP(1-90), full-length ZitP, or binding-deficient mutants.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C99 are supported by overexpression experiments with time-lapse imaging (Figure 4D), population-level phenotyping (Figure 4E-F), and appropriate controls including W35I mutants and non-membrane-anchored versions. The requirement for membrane anchoring is demonstrated by domain swap experiments with MalF-TM (Figure 4F).

results.result: The PopZ-ZitP bipolarization system is conserved and modular across α-proteobacteria. Orthologous ZitP and PopZ proteins from Brevundimonas diminuta and Rickettsia massiliae function interchangeably with C. crescentus components in both C. crescentus and E. coli, maintaining the structure-function relationship including W35-dependent binding.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C44-C45, C102-C109 are supported by extensive heterologous expression experiments (Figures 6A-G) demonstrating functional conservation across distantly related species. The modularity is shown by mix-and-match experiments with components from different organisms, and the W35 requirement is conserved (Figure 6C).

results.result: ChIP-Seq experiments revealed that ParB exclusively occupies the parS centromere site, while the ZitP•PopZ complex associates with two chromosomal regions flanking parS by 2-3 kbp. The ParAB interaction sites in PopZ are critical for this association of ZitP•PopZ with parS-flanking regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C79, C120-C121 are supported by ChIP-Seq data (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) showing distinct binding patterns for ParB versus ZitP. The requirement for PopZ-ParAB interaction is demonstrated by loss of ZitP association in PopZ mutants. However, the mechanism underlying this indirect association remains unclear.

results.result: Orthologous ZitP(1-90) variants from multiple α-proteobacteria show identical polar localization in C. crescentus. R. sphaeroides ZitP(1-43) shows weak polar localization due to a naturally-occurring Q27 substitution in the basic patch; 'correcting' this to Q27R restores robust polar localization, which is again lost with the W35I mutation.
results.evaluation: Claims C55, C74-C76 are supported by localization experiments with orthologs from multiple species (Figures 1E, 3C-D) and site-directed mutagenesis of R. sphaeroides ZitP. The rescue of localization by Q27R and its loss with W35I provides strong evidence for the importance of the basic patch, with appropriate protein abundance controls (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).

results.result: The zinc-finger domain from the unrelated AgmX protein from the δ-proteobacterium Myxococcus xanthus is not polar in C. crescentus, indicating divergence from the ZitP ZnR family.
results.evaluation: Claim C56 is supported by localization experiments (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) showing diffuse localization of AgmX ZnR in C. crescentus. This negative control strengthens the specificity of the ZitP ZnR-PopZ interaction, though the structural basis for the difference is not explored.

results.result: mCherry-PopZ co-localizes with Dendra2-ZitP(1-43) in C. crescentus cells. When PopZ is overexpressed, both Dendra2-ZitP(1-43) and full-length Dendra2-ZitP adopt a monopolar 'plug'-like disposition, suggesting recruitment to PopZ aggregates.
results.evaluation: Claims C59 and C62 are supported by co-localization microscopy (Figures 1H, 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A). The 'plug' phenotype is consistent with known PopZ overexpression behavior and provides additional evidence for direct interaction, though the biological relevance of this artificial condition is limited.

results.result: A C. crescentus strain with a Tn5-GFP insertion in zitP expresses a bipolarly localized truncated ZitP-GFP fusion and is viable. ZitP is not essential for viability but is required for pilus biogenesis and motility. The predicted ZitP protein contains an N-terminal ZnR domain (residues 1-37), a transmembrane segment (residues 106-127), and a C-terminal DUF3426 domain (residues 128-245), with the DUF3426 required for pilus biogenesis but not for polar localization.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C51 are supported by prior Tn-Seq data (cited), domain predictions, and functional analysis. The bipolar localization of the truncated fusion (Figure 1D) and the dispensability of DUF3426 for localization are demonstrated. However, these are largely confirmatory of previous work rather than novel findings.

results.result: The C-terminal DUF3426 domain is not required to rescue growth defects in ΔzitP ΔpopZ cells expressing mCherry-PopZKE, as ZitP(1-133) is sufficient. However, when PopZ binding is abrogated (W35I mutation), cells grow poorly. No ZitP dependency is observed in ΔpopZ cells expressing unmodified PopZ.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C88 are supported by growth curve measurements (Figure 4C) with appropriate genetic controls. The differential requirement for ZitP depending on PopZ functionality demonstrates specificity, though the growth assays could benefit from additional replicates and statistical analysis.

results.result: Overproduction of ZitP(1-133) in mCherry-popZKEP cells (impaired in ParAB interaction) recapitulates the overexpression phenotype seen in cells with wild-type mCherry-PopZ.
results.evaluation: Claim C100 is supported by localization microscopy (Figure 4G) showing similar phenotypes in PopZKEP and wild-type PopZ backgrounds. This demonstrates that ZitP overexpression effects are independent of PopZ-ParAB interaction, though the sample size and quantification are limited.

results.result: Inactivation of ZitP has a mild effect on CFP-ParB localization in wild-type C. crescentus cells.
results.evaluation: Claim C80 is supported by quantification of ParB localization (Figure 4—figure supplement 2). The 'mild' effect is appropriately characterized as the phenotype is subtle in the wild-type background, becoming more pronounced only when PopZ-ParAB interaction is impaired.

results.result: Background information on bacterial polarity, the α-proteobacterial lineage, C. crescentus cell biology, chromosome segregation, and PopZ function. These claims establish the context for the study, including the observation that most α-proteobacterial genomes encode PopZ and ParAB but not TipN, suggesting TipN-independent control mechanisms exist.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C8-C35 represent established knowledge from the literature, appropriately cited throughout. These provide necessary background but are not novel findings of this study. The inference about TipN-independent mechanisms (C30) is reasonable given the genomic distribution data.

results.result: The ZitP ZnR acts as a conserved polar localization sequence analogous to eukaryotic nuclear localization signals, promoting interaction with the PopZ polar organizer. ZitP emerges as a new component of the α-proteobacterial polarity control pathway.
results.evaluation: Claims C110-C111, C116 represent the conceptual framing and significance of the findings. The analogy to NLS is appropriate given the functional similarity (targeting to a specific cellular location via protein-protein interaction), and the designation of ZitP as a 'new component' is justified by the novel characterization, though ZitP was previously known.

results.result: PopZ localization is regulated by redundant mechanisms in C. crescentus, with one mechanism potentially requiring ParAB or depending on the N-terminal region of PopZ that promotes interaction with ParAB and other client proteins.
results.evaluation: Claims C113-C114 represent interpretations of the genetic data showing synthetic phenotypes. The redundancy is well-supported, though the exact nature of the ParAB-dependent mechanism remains somewhat speculative ('may require'). The interpretation is reasonable but could benefit from more direct mechanistic evidence.

results.result: ZitP is bifunctional, with the C-terminal DUF3426 controlling pilus biogenesis (less conserved) and the membrane-anchored ZnR controlling PopZ localization (conserved in Rickettsiae). The ZnR function is featured by many ZitP orthologs from obligate intracellular α-proteobacteria.
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C119 synthesize findings about ZitP domain functions. The bifunctionality is supported by domain deletion analysis and conservation patterns (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A). However, the claim about 'many' rickettsial orthologs is based on limited experimental testing (primarily R. massiliae).

results.result: ZitP is well-positioned to control ParB•parS dynamics and can impair segregation by sequestering the centromere into aberrant PopZ•ZitP clusters. This function depends on membrane-anchored ZitP ZnR interaction with PopZ, potentially targeting residues flanking the conserved C-terminal DUF2497 of PopZ.
results.evaluation: Claims C122-C124 represent mechanistic interpretations of the overexpression and ChIP-Seq data. While the positioning near parS is demonstrated (C120-C121) and overexpression causes segregation defects (C92-C93), the specific mechanism of 'sequestering' and the exact PopZ binding site remain incompletely characterized. The DUF2497 targeting is inferred from deletion analysis but lacks direct structural evidence.

results.result: The DUF2497 region may serve as a key determinant in PopZ to regulate its association with client proteins and its bipolar localization and/or dynamics.
results.evaluation: Claim C125 is speculative ('may serve'), based on the observation that ZitP interacts with PopZ independently of the N-terminal region. While reasonable, this hypothesis lacks direct experimental support such as DUF2497 mutagenesis or structural characterization of the ZitP-PopZ interface.

results.result: The α-proteobacterial PopZ system differs from the Firmicutes DivIVA system in ancestry and mechanism. PopZ forms sporadic monopolar and cytoplasmic clusters in E. coli without ZitP, but with ZitP forms robust bipolar complexes at the polar membrane (observed by PALM). This bipolarization can be reconstituted with components from different α-proteobacteria and is unlikely to be mediated by specialized phospholipids.
results.evaluation: Claims C126-C130 compare PopZ to DivIVA and characterize the heterologous system behavior. The PALM data (Figure 5C) clearly shows polar membrane localization, and the cross-species reconstitution (Figures 6D-G) supports modularity. The argument against phospholipid-mediated localization is logical but indirect, based on compositional differences rather than direct testing.

results.result: Rickettsial ZitP retains PopZ control activities, suggesting obligate intracellular pathogens feature a polarized PopZ•ZitP complex. The PopZ•ZitP system may have served as a primordial platform for acquiring specialized polarity functions via PopZ-interacting proteins.
results.evaluation: Claims C131-C133 represent evolutionary interpretations. The functional conservation in rickettsial proteins is demonstrated (Figures 6A-G), supporting the inference about obligate intracellular pathogens. The 'primordial platform' hypothesis (C133) is speculative but reasonable given the conservation pattern and the known polarization of rickettsial Sca2.

results.result: PopZ has diverse functions across α-proteobacterial lineages including stalk biogenesis in C. crescentus and unipolar growth in Rhizobiales. In Rhizobiales, PopZ is unipolar and ZitP orthologs are absent, suggesting unknown control mechanisms. In Rhodobacterales, many members lack PopZ orthologs, and ZitP ZnR structural divergence suggests appropriation for other functions.
results.evaluation: Claims C134-C138 discuss evolutionary diversification of the system, appropriately citing prior work. The inferences about unknown mechanisms in Rhizobiales (C136) and functional divergence in Rhodobacterales (C138) are reasonable based on genomic and structural observations, though they remain speculative without direct experimental evidence.

results.result: Proper polarity control is critical for cellular fitness. In yeast, misregulated polarity complexes impair fitness to the extent that complete elimination is favored over improper regulation. Similar selective forces likely ensured evolution and retention of polarity control modules in bacteria, as misregulation perturbs the α-proteobacterial cell division cycle.
results.evaluation: Claims C139-C141 provide evolutionary context, with C140 citing yeast work and C141 drawing parallels to bacteria. The inference about selective forces (C141) is reasonable given the demonstrated cell division defects upon ZitP misregulation, though it remains somewhat speculative ('must have ensured').
